world_behind.title: Seeds first
world_behind.text: The chapter opens with the camp's ordinary work: "all manner of seeds of every kind" (v. 1) gathered for a country nobody has seen. The record's rhythm sets grain next to visions without embarrassment; the family prepares for the promised land with both.

cites.quote: all manner of seeds of every kind

spans.text: all manner of seeds of every kind

world_behind.title: "Dreamed a dream" is dream-language
world_behind.text: The doubling, "I have dreamed a dream" (v. 2), is an old Hebrew way of saying it (Joseph and Pharaoh dream their dreams the same way), and Lehi's correction, "or, in other words, I have seen a vision" (v. 2), makes a claim: in this family the night dream and the prophetic vision are one instrument, not two.

cites.quote: I have dreamed a dream

spans.text: I have dreamed a dream

cites.quote: or, in other words, I have seen a vision

spans.text: or, in other words, I have seen a vision

world_behind.title: A desert man's images
world_behind.text: Waste, field, river, mist, and a path along the water: the dream is furnished from the family's own country. Desert wadis breed sudden fogs, rivers run banked by traveler's paths, and a guide-rail through bad ground was a thing caravan hands could picture. Revelation speaks in local material.

world_behind.title: The guide in white
world_behind.text: Vision literature of the age begins this way: a luminous figure who arrives before the seeing starts and bids the seer follow (Ezekiel and Daniel both meet such guides). Lehi's dream keeps the convention, and note that following the guide leads first into darkness, not out of it.

world_behind.title: The building the family would know
world_behind.text: Fine dress, mixed crowds, height, and scorn: the great and spacious building reads like the great houses of Jerusalem the family had just left: the urban establishment seen from a tent, elevated, ungrounded, and laughing.

world_behind.title: The tree of life had a long history
world_behind.text: Eden's tree stood planted in the garden's midst, behind a guarded way (Gen. 2:9; 3:24); Proverbs made wisdom itself a tree of life to them that lay hold on her (Prov. 3:18); and the Revelation of John promises its fruit to the faithful (Rev. 2:7). Lehi's version is distinctive: no guarded gate, no waiting for the end, but a tree reachable now, by families, on foot.

words.text: Dream grammar: "methought I saw in my dream, a dark and dreary wilderness" (v. 4). It is the same careful hedge the record used for Lehi's first vision, "he thought he saw" (1 Ne. 1:8): a family habit of refusing to claim more precision than seeing gives. The care is itself a credential: witnesses who mark the edges of their knowledge can be trusted inside them.

cites.quote: methought I saw in my dream, a dark and dreary wilderness

spans.text: methought I saw in my dream, a dark and dreary wilderness

words.text: "I beckoned unto them" (v. 15): a gesture before it is a sentence, joined to "a loud voice" (v. 15). The dream's evangelism is bodily: a father at a tree, waving his family in, calling across a field. Nothing in the scene compels; everything in it invites, and the posture becomes the record's standing image for how truth recruits.

cites.quote: I beckoned unto them

spans.text: I beckoned unto them

cites.quote: a loud voice

spans.text: a loud voice

words.text: Not a wall but weather: "an exceedingly great mist of darkness" (v. 23) that rises after travelers have "commence in the path" (v. 22). Mist blinds gradually, disorients, and lifts nowhere in the dream. The word chooses the hazard's character: what defeats path-walkers is the slow loss of bearings.

cites.quote: an exceedingly great mist of darkness

spans.text: an exceedingly great mist of darkness

spans.text: commence in the path

words.text: The second company comes through the mist "clinging to the rod of iron" (v. 24), and still ends ashamed and lost, while the later multitude comes "continually holding fast" (v. 30) and falls down to eat. The dream distinguishes two grips on the same rod: the clutch of crisis and the settled hold of habit. Only one survives arrival.

words.text: Roads are "strange roads" (v. 32) and the building is "that strange building" (v. 33): estranged, foreign to the field's purpose. The word quietly maps the dream's moral geography: everything not oriented to the tree is not merely other ground; it is alien ground.

spans.text: strange roads

phrases.text: The dream opens in the family's own address: they are camped in a wilderness while Lehi dreams one. Four verses later it is a "dark and dreary waste" (v. 7) he must cross himself. The vision does not spare the visionary the terrain; even the man who will stand at the tree begins in the dark, hours deep.

cites.quote: dark and dreary waste

spans.text: dark and dreary waste

phrases.term: The multitude of his tender mercies
phrases.text: The book's thesis phrase (1 Ne. 1:20) surfaces inside the dream, as prayer: mercy asked "according to the multitude of his tender mercies" (v. 8), and the darkness gives way to the field. Even in symbolic country the record's mechanics hold: the waste is exited by petition.

cites.quote: according to the multitude of his tender mercies

spans.text: according to the multitude of his tender mercies

phrases.text: The fruit is measured on the scale of wanting: desirable to make one happy, desirable above all. The dream's psychology is exact: what the tree offers is sweetness, and the only recorded reaction to tasting it is the wish that others taste it. Desire, rightly aimed, is the dream's engine.

Introduced without explanation: iron, grippable, unbending, cold, running along the bank of a river, ending at the tree. The record withholds the key for three more chapters (1 Ne. 11:25), letting the reader hold the raw symbol the way the travelers hold the rod: before understanding it.

The dream's counter-tree: it "stood as it were in the air, high above the earth" (v. 26), with no foundation, no field, no fruit. It is full anyway. Its census is complete (old and young, male and female, finely dressed) and its single activity is scorn. The shape carries the meaning: the tree is rooted and low, the building hangs, and everything hanging falls.

cites.quote: stood as it were in the air, high above the earth

spans.text: stood as it were in the air, high above the earth

phrases.text: The dream's entire defensive doctrine in four words. No rebuttal of the mockers, no counter-scorn, no engagement at all; heed is the only thing the building can collect, and withholding it is the whole discipline. The record states it as the difference between those who stayed at the tree and those who fell away ashamed.

verses.label: v. 4–9
verses.title: Hours in the dark first
verses.text: The guide bids Lehi follow, and what comes next is "a dark and dreary waste" (v. 7), for "the space of many hours" (v. 8). The dream's first teaching is its pacing: even guided travel passes through unexplained darkness. The way out is a prayer for mercy.

cites.quote: a dark and dreary waste

spans.text: a dark and dreary waste

cites.quote: the space of many hours

spans.text: the space of many hours

verses.label: v. 10–12
verses.title: Tasting turns outward
verses.text: The fruit fills Lehi's soul "with exceedingly great joy" (v. 12), and the joy's first motion reaches outward: "I began to be desirous that my family should partake of it also" (v. 12). The dream tests every reader with Lehi's reflex: joy that does not immediately reach for others is not yet the tree's joy.

cites.quote: I began to be desirous that my family should partake of it also

verses.label: v. 13–18
verses.title: The family sorts itself
verses.text: At his call, Sariah, Sam, and Nephi come and eat; Laman and Lemuel "would not come unto me and partake of the fruit" (v. 18). The verse is the caravan's rebellion (1 Ne. 7) replayed in symbols, and the refusal happens in full sight of the tree. Distance was never the brothers' problem.

cites.quote: would not come unto me and partake of the fruit

spans.text: would not come unto me and partake of the fruit

verses.label: v. 21–25
verses.title: Two companies, two endings
verses.text: The first multitude takes the path without the rod and is lost in mist before reaching anything. The second clings, arrives, tastes, and then "they did cast their eyes about as if they were ashamed" (v. 25). The dream's hardest demography: arrival is a checkpoint, not a destination, and the tree can be abandoned from beside it.

cites.quote: they did cast their eyes about as if they were ashamed

spans.text: they did cast their eyes about as if they were ashamed

verses.label: v. 26–28
verses.title: The building goes to work
verses.text: Scorn is the second weather of the dream: where mist blinds the path, mockery works the tree itself. Those who fall are embarrassed away, "ashamed, because of those that were scoffing at them" (v. 28). The building never touches anyone; it only points.

cites.quote: ashamed, because of those that were scoffing at them

spans.text: ashamed, because of those that were scoffing at them

verses.label: v. 30
verses.title: The grip that ends kneeling
verses.text: The other multitude presses forward "continually holding fast to the rod of iron" (v. 30), and their arrival is different in posture as well as outcome: they "fell down and partook of the fruit of the tree" (v. 30). Falling down is worship's shape. The dream's survivors reach the tree as petitioners.

cites.quote: fell down and partook of the fruit of the tree

verses.label: v. 35–38
verses.title: The dream ends in parenting
verses.text: Lehi surfaces from the vision afraid, and the record slows over his response: he exhorted "with all the feeling of a tender parent" (v. 37), preached, prophesied, bade them keep the commandments, and then "he did cease speaking" (v. 38). The last verb is the hardest one in the chapter: even a seer's persuasion has an end, and what remains after ceasing is the sons' own choice.

spans.text: he did cease speaking

chapter.title: A vision deployed as an intervention
chapter.text: The dream is framed before and after by fear for two named sons (v. 4, 36): Lehi tells it as parenting, with its worst news saved for last: "Laman and Lemuel partook not of the fruit, said my father" (v. 35). Whatever else the dream is, in this chapter it is a father's plea with the ending left open.

cites.quote: Laman and Lemuel partook not of the fruit, said my father

spans.text: Laman and Lemuel partook not of the fruit, said my father

chapter.title: Symbols before keys
chapter.text: The record hands the reader raw images (tree, rod, mist, building) and withholds every interpretation for three chapters (1 Ne. 11–12; 15). The sequencing is deliberate pedagogy: the reader must walk the dream uninterpreted, as Lehi did, and the meanings arrive later only for those who, like Nephi, go ask. Experience precedes explanation in this record's theory of revelation.

chapter.title: Four companies, one difference
chapter.text: No-rod walkers lost in mist; clingers who arrive and fall to shame; holders-fast who arrive kneeling; building-seekers who never wanted the tree. What sorts them is never speed, distance, or starting place. It is each company's relationship to the rod and to the scorn. The dream sorts its people by how they hold on.

chapter.title: Falling after tasting
chapter.text: The dream's pattern break, twice stated (v. 25, 28): people who genuinely reached the tree, genuinely ate, and were then embarrassed off the field. Nothing in the chapter is more unnerving or more pastorally aimed: the dream refuses to let arrival function as security, and the record will spend whole books on people who tasted and left.

chapter.title: Rooted versus suspended
chapter.text: The tree stands planted by living water; the building "stood as it were in the air" (v. 26). The dream's two destinations differ less in population than in physics: one is grounded and bears fruit, the other is elevated, foundationless, and produces nothing but noise. Height without ground is the dream's definition of pride, three chapters before the angel says so (1 Ne. 11:36).

cites.quote: stood as it were in the air

spans.text: stood as it were in the air

chapter.title: The vision cycle opens
chapter.text: This dream generates the whole unit: chapter 10 hands it to Nephi, chapters 11–14 expand it into world-history, chapter 15 watches the brothers decline to ask about it. The unit's real subject is announced here in miniature: what each hearer does with another man's revelation.

chapter.title: The family map, read twice
chapter.text: Lehi reads the dream as the present tense of his household: two sons at the tree, two refusing. The record, written decades later, reads it as the founding map of two nations. Both readings stand, and the second gives the first its weight: family choices in this book are never merely domestic.

applications.title: Pray sooner in the waste
applications.text: Lehi traveled hours dark before asking for mercy. Locate your own current waste, the dry calling or the unanswered stretch, and move the prayer up: the field appeared after the petition.

applications.title: Keep a beckon list
applications.text: Joy's first motion at the tree was an invitation. Write the names you would actually wave toward what feeds you, and this month make the gesture for one of them plainly enough that it is recognizably a beckon and not a hint.

applications.title: Choose the settled grip
applications.text: Clinging is what crisis does; holding fast continually is what habit does. Convert one crisis-only spiritual practice into a fixed daily hold, same time, same place, no renegotiation, and let the rod bear weight before the next mist, not during it.

applications.title: Rehearse heeding not
applications.text: The building's whole arsenal is attention. Name the specific scorn that currently reaches you (the account, the voice, the room) and decide in advance what "we heeded them not" looks like there. Shame that is pre-decided against collects nothing.

applications.title: Arrive kneeling
applications.text: The survivors fell down before they partook. Put the posture back into your receiving: thanks said before the blessing is used, sacrament taken as petitioners rather than customers, answers received on knees that asked.

applications.title: Exhort tenderly, then trust the ceasing
applications.text: Lehi gave his hardest warning with a tender parent's whole feeling, and then stopped speaking. For the person you cannot persuade: match his order. Say the true thing with visible love, and then let silence and agency do the work speech cannot.

questions.text: What dark and dreary stretch am I currently in, and have I prayed from inside it or only endured it?
When something last filled me with joy, who did I beckon? If no one, what does that say about the fruit I was eating?
Who in my family can see the tree from where they stand and still will not come, and has my beckoning stayed tender, or turned to pressure?
Which mist is currently costing me my bearings: what rose gradually enough that I did not name it a hazard?
Where have I already tasted something true and let embarrassment loosen my hold on it?
Whose pointing finger do I still heed, and what would it honestly cost me to stop?
Is there a place where my exhorting is done and the next faithful act is to cease speaking?
